articles.text: Piedmont students started the school year on a Monday this year, August 12, after years of confusing mid-week starting days. At Beach, Wildwood and Havens elementary schools a healthy percentage of parents walked their young scholars to campus on Day 1 of the new school year to take dozens of photos of new outfits, haircuts and backpacks. For kids starting school for the very first time, entering Transitional Kindergarten or Kindergarten at 8:30 a.m., parents put aside many common thoughts of work, dinner, bills and everything else to focus on their kids’ first day of school. In such a kidsfirst community, the beginning of the school year brings forth a substantial synchronicity. Students entering Beach School on Lake Avenue walked through a balloon arch of purple and white to see their school’s new playground. At Wildwood, a ceremonial flag- raising ceremony on campus captivated the crowd of parents and students alike. At Havens, kids posed with friends reunited and lined up in single file order for the first time since May. At Havens the steady hand of Principal Anne Dolid led a smooth opening day of the school year. At Beach School, Anne Valva looks more and more at home in the principal’s office in her third year. Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond enters her second year eager to continue the work she began one year ago. The first day of school always brings the possibility of tears from any of Piedmont’s students, parents and siblings at the big change on hand. Nearly all welcomed the new beginning however and the school year in Piedmont has officially begun. For the duration of August, all elementary kids in grades 1-3 will be released from school at 2:00 p.m. This time allows time for teacher assessments. Teachers will be in touch with families to schedule appointments after 2:00 p.m. In September a regular schedule resumes with 3:00 p.m. release times (except Wednesdays) for kids in grades 1-5. (See additional photos in the School Section.)

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has partnered with Ava Community Energy (formerly East Bay Community Energy) to offer an induction burner borrowing program for residents at no cost to the public. Those interested in the Cooktop Lending Program may inquire at the planning and building department front counter at City Hall, Monday-Thursday from 8:30 a.m. - 12 p.m. and 1 p.m. - 5 p.m. to sign up. “The Induction Cooktop Lending Program is a way for East Bay residents to borrow and ‘test drive’ induction cooking in their home for free,” according to the company’s website. “This program is available to all East Bay residents—Ava customers as well as non-Ava customers who receive electric service from PG&E.” Induction burners have been receiving increased attention from home cooks in recent years. Induction appliances are up to three times more efficient than gas stoves, and up to 10% more efficient than conventional smooth top electric ranges according to the Department of Energy. However, many consumers have been slow to embrace them because of the high start-up costs related to converting from gas or electric ranges. The Induction Lending Kit includes a portable induction cooktop, a compatible pan, cooktop operating instructions, recipes and a carrying bag. Residents may also choose between a classic sauté pan and a wok at the time of loan. Induction Lending Kits may be reserved for free at www.tinyurl. com/ava-induction. Burners and cookware may be borrowed for up to two weeks at a time. Wait times to receive burners and cookware may be up to one week. For more information, contact the City of Piedmont Planning and Building Department at 420-3050. articles.text: Pixar studio and artists, former Alameda County Board of Supervisors Member Wilma Chan among those to be honored George Mark Children’s House (GMCH), as part of its 20th-anniversary celebration, will present its first-ever Hummingbird Awards in a ceremony today, August 14, to pay tribute to several individuals and organizations that have played a pivotal role in helping the pediatric hospice provide exceptional care to seriously ill children and support for their families. The ceremony will be held at 11 a.m. at George Mark Children’s House, 2121 George Mark Lane, in San Leandro. The Hummingbird Awards will be part of a re-dedication ceremony for George Mark’s restorative garden, Hummingbird Hill. Hummingbirds hold a special place in the hearts of the community at George Mark Children’s House, symbolizing healing, comfort, and hope. Kathy Hull, founder of George Mark Children’s House, will present the awards with CEO Shekinah Eliassen. Pixar Animation Studios will receive an award for its ongoing commitment and robust volunteer engagement with the organization over the years. “Pixar Animation Studios exemplifies corporate citizenship at its finest, making a meaningful difference in the lives of George Mark patients and their families,” reads a press release from the George Mark Children’s House. The Honorable Wilma Chan, former Alameda County Supervisor, will be honored posthumously at the ceremony. Chan, a distinguished advocate and early champion of George Mark Children’s House, played a pivotal role in the organization’s foundational years. Chan’s former Chief of Staff Rachel Richman will accept the award on her behalf. Alameda County District 3 Supervisor Lena Tam and District 3 Director Silin Huang will also be in attendance. Wilma Chan passed away on November 3, 2021, after she was struck by a vehicle while walking her dog near the intersection of Shoreline Drive and Grand Street in Alameda. Shekinah Eliassen, CEO of George Mark Children’s House, holds a Hummingbird Award. Hummingbird Hill, George Mark Children’s House’s restorative garden, is due for a re-dedication at the awards ceremony. Photos by George Mark Children’s House The first-ever Hummingbird Awards were designed by Pixar artists and cast from bronze by local metalworkers at ArtWorks Foundry. Bob Pauley and Jerome Ranft of Pixar Animation Studios will also receive awards. These distinguished artists – whose work is featured in films Toy Story, Finding Nemo, and Cars – have generously contributed their time, sketches, illustrations and maquettes of hummingbirds to George Mark Children’s House pro bono over the years. Cody Lyon of Pixar Animation Studios (Elemental, Coco) will also be awarded. Lyon is a familiar presence at George Mark events, where he creates animated versions of families as part of memory-building activities. He also designed and created a stunning mural in the GMCH Art Room as a poignant tribute to a bereaved family. Serpico Landscaping will receive an award for generously providing pro bono landscaping services to the GMCH for over 15 years, ensuring the gardens and Hummingbird Hill are meticulously maintained. Kambiz Mehrafshani of ArtWorks Foundry, one of the nation’s leading foundries for the production and restoration of bronze sculptures, reliefs and monuments, will also receive an award. Kambiz has been instrumental in producing the exquisite Pixar-designed bronze statues that will be presented as awards for the Hummingbird Awards, further enhancing the legacy of compassion and artistry at GMCH. articles.text: Wistaria Way project specifically does not qualify for SB 9 Mayor Jen Cavanagh has long been a vocal advocate for the environment, consistently highlighting the importance of protecting Piedmont’s natural assets. However, her environmental commitment faces a significant test with a looming decision: Will the city council endorse a developer’s proposal for construction on 77 Wistaria Way, or will it require City staff to comply with Piedmont law and enforce the state and city regulations under SB 9 written to protect the environment? Unless the city council steps in and requires city staff to process the project in compliance with local environmental law, Piedmont will find out by July 16 when construction is set to begin at 77 Wistaria Way. Piedmont’s City staff chose to bypass the Planning Commission’s review of the 77 Wistaria Way project and process it under the State’s SB 9 regulation, which allowed the project to be processed ministerially – by the staff behind closed doors with neither Planning Commission nor public visibility or input. However, per California state law and local Piedmont Code, due to the environmental characteristics of the 77 Wistaria Way property, the project specifically does not qualify for SB 9. According to California state law and local Piedmont law, lots which contain streams, wetland soil or wetland vegetation as defined in Piedmont City Code (Sec. 17.54.050.B 1) and California State Law (SB9) are ineligible for SB9 development. Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact well-known to the local community. Many neighbors have actively raised their concerns regarding the staff’s noncompliant decision to process the developer’s application under the expedited and not transparent SB 9 process. Planning staff and City Council received formal notice of the staff’s non-compliance with SB 9 as early as August 23, 2023 – four months prior to the City’s decision to approve the developer’s land-use permit on December 27, 2024. Following the approval of the land use permit, Piedmont residents wrote multiple additional related letters to the city; however, City staff have largely dismissed residents’ concerns, maintaining the site qualifies for processing under SB 9. On June 17 neighbors spoke during the public forum of the city council meeting; the following week they presented a petition to the City, with notice to the developer, requesting to be on the City Council agenda; and again raised their concerns in the July 1 city council meeting. However, the residents’ significant and repeated efforts to urge city council to require City staff to comply with state and local law fell on deaf ears. Piedmont city staff quietly approved building permits for the project last week on July 2. The first offer from the city to engage with residents on the topic came one day later on July 3. It was the day of the Piedmont Post’s first article on this issue, and one day after the City had approved building permits. A meeting between staff and concerned neighbors took place on July 5th. During this meeting, staff asserted confidence in their understanding of the land’s environmental aspects, citing a report from a “licensed biologist” – paid for by the developer – who gave reasons outside the scope of relevant state and local law for why he felt the project should not be disqualified from SB 9 consideration. Despite the developer’s biologist admitting the site contained multiple of the criteria, which would disqualify the project for SB 9 processed, City staff dismissed the neighbors’ claims about the creek, without citing any specifics from the report, only explaining that a report by a “licensed biologist” must be accurate because such a professional would not want to run the risk of losing their license for producing a flawed report. The California License website reveals that “biologist” is not a professional category that holds a license to practice in the state. This situation presents a critical question: Will the city council require staff to comply with the City’s own law, or will the developer’s interests prevail? This question is increasingly important as the city expects to see an increasing number of SB 9 applications, which lowers the bar for developers and often more significant impacts on neighbors.
articles.title: Will the City Council hold its staff accountable to the law?

Wistaria Way project specifically does not qualify for SB 9 By David Ashton Mayor Jen Cavanagh has long been a vocal advocate for the environment, consistently highlighting the importance of protecting Piedmont’s natural assets. However, her environmental commitment faces a significant test with a looming decision: Will the city council endorse a developer’s proposal for construction on 77 Wistaria Way, or will it require City staff to comply with Piedmont law and enforce the state and city regulations under SB 9 written to protect the environment? Unless the city council steps in and requires city staff to process the project in compliance with local environmental law, Piedmont will find out by July 16 when construction is set to begin at 77 Wistaria Way. Piedmont’s City staff chose to bypass the Planning Commission’s review of the 77 Wistaria Way project and process it under the State’s SB 9 regulation, which allowed the project to be processed ministerially – by the staff behind closed doors with neither Planning Commission nor public visibility or input. However, per California state law and local Piedmont Code, due to the environmental characteristics of the 77 Wistaria Way property, the project specifically does not qualify for SB 9. According to California state law and local Piedmont law, lots which contain streams, wetland soil or wetland vegetation as defined in Piedmont City Code (Sec. 17.54.050.B 1) and California State Law (SB9) are ineligible for SB9 development. Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact well-known to the local community. Many neighbors have actively raised their concerns regarding the staff’s noncompliant decision to process the developer’s application under the expedited and not transparent SB 9 process. Planning staff and City Council received formal notice of the staff’s non-compliance with SB 9 as early as August 23, 2023 – four months prior to the City’s decision to approve the developer’s land-use permit on December 27, 2024. Following the approval of the land use permit, Piedmont residents wrote multiple additional related letters to the city; however, City staff have largely dismissed residents’ concerns, maintaining the site qualifies for processing under SB 9. On June 17 neighbors spoke during the public forum of the city council meeting; the following week they presented a petition to the City, with notice to the developer, requesting to be on the City Council agenda; and again raised their concerns in the July 1 city council meeting. However, the residents’ significant and repeated efforts to urge city council to require City staff to comply with state and local law fell on deaf ears. Piedmont city staff quietly approved building permits for the project last week on July 2. The first offer from the city to engage with residents on the topic came one day later on July 3. It was the day of the Piedmont Post’s first article on this issue, and one day after the City had approved building permits. A meeting between staff and concerned neighbors took place on July 5th. During this meeting, staff asserted confidence in their understanding of the land’s environmental aspects, citing a report from a “licensed biologist” – paid for by the developer – who gave reasons outside the scope of relevant state and local law for why he felt the project should not be disqualified from SB 9 consideration. Despite the developer’s biologist admitting the site contained multiple of the criteria, which would disqualify the project for SB 9 processed, City staff dismissed the neighbors’ claims about the creek, without citing any specifics from the report, only explaining that a report by a “licensed biologist” must be accurate because such a professional would not want to run the risk of losing their license for producing a flawed report. The California License website reveals that “biologist” is not a professional category that holds a license to practice in the state. This situation presents a critical question: Will the city council require staff to comply with the City’s own law, or will the developer’s interests prevail? This question is increasingly important as the city expects to see an increasing number of SB 9 applications, which lowers the bar for developers and often more significant impacts on neighbors.

articles.text: A look at the possible future of housing in Piedmont is not pretty The developers’ previous involvement in a housing project in San Francisco has residents worried that something similar could happen in Piedmont. A new housing project on Wistaria Way, located at 77 Wistaria Way, has sparked resident concerns that unchecked development could harm their neighborhoods in the near future. Using the framework of SB9 to justify housing projects does not bode well for the city according to nearby residents and a growing chorus of opponents. Residents have repeatedly expressed dissatisfaction with the city government for a lack of transparency during the planning phase and raised questions about what the future of Piedmont will look like under recently passed California housing laws. What happened? The construction project at 77 Wistaria Way aims to divide a vacant lot into two parcels. Property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead, the developers, propose to build a new home on each parcel, as well as a third house as an accessory dwelling unit (ADU). The project’s application was approved by Piedmont’s Planning Department on December 27, 2023. On July 16 this summer- contractors from Gregorio Tree Service began cutting down trees on the property in the heavily wooded cul-de-sac of Wistaria. Controversial new state law SB9 (Senate Bill 9), also known as the California Housing Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, continues to be a contentious issue in Piedmont. Beginning on January 1, 2022, the state decreed that homeowners can build up to four homes on an existing parcel. According to UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation, this state law effectively eliminates single-family zoning. The law allows the owner to “split” their lot, making it easier to sell or finance additional homes on the same parcel. While supporters believe the law will help address California’s current housing crisis by creating new opportunities for small-scale home building, opponents of SB9 are concerned that it will lead to speculation and unchecked growth at the expense of a community’s character and traditions. Many members of the community have expressed outrage over the plans for the Wistaria Way project. “When I bought my home, I had the guarantee of a single-family-zoned lot. I never anticipated high-density housing Photo by Staff Photos A portion of the creek runs through the properties around Wistaria Way. City officials and residents disagree on whether it qualifies as protected wetlands. A 3D rendering of what the project at 77 Wistaria Way may look like. in my backyard. And now, that’s what I’m getting,” said David Ashton, a third-generation Piedmont resident whose property borders the project. Residents have also complained that the Wistaria project’s three additional homes show no plans for a built-in garage, a move that will make parking scarce on an already narrow 14-foot wide road. “I don’t feel like City Council and staff appreciate that SB9 lot splits are not a desired outcome to the current residents and citizens,” said Rich Latvala, who also lives near the project. Possible wetlands on property Residents and city officials also disagree over the presence of protected wetlands on the property. Residents contend that the construction site at 77 Wistaria Way contains a section of Wildwood Creek which flows through many of their yards and that construction would interfere with the creek. Protected wetlands are considered an exception to SB9, and many residents insist that this should have precluded the Wistaria project’s application from approval. The Planning Department disagrees. “The project was found to be compliant with all state and city regulations under SB9 and our own city code,” said Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “These findings were based on the information provided, which included a report from a licensed biologist that determined that there were no wetlands on the site.” The biologist, he confirmed was hired by the property owners of 77 Wistaria Way. Lack of transparency City officials have said at several public meetings that the owners’ application for a lot split was approved via “ministerial approval,” meaning there was no public review of the building design. This has upset many residents, who believe it is a move away from the city’s usually transparent review practices. “This revised project seems to have avoided the obligatory planning review process that all residents live by under the pretense that it qualifies for SB9. This project will set a precedent for the misuse or application of SB9 in Piedmont that will open the door for unchecked and unreviewed development, degrading the character and standards that make Piedmont the city that it is today,” said Latvala. Some residents also believe that SB9, as it is currently being enforced, lacks refinement. For example, SB9 requires owner occupancy for all lot split developments. The owner must sign an affidavit stating they intend to live in one of the units as their primary residence for at least three years after approval. This requirement is intended to prevent developers from buying lots and splitting them and to maintain affordable housing options for the public. articles.text: For many children, the journey through school is a time of discovery, learning, and growth. However, for those with speech and language disorders, this journey can be fraught with challenges that impact their academic performance and overall school experience. Understanding the profound effects these disorders have on a child’s educational journey is crucial for parents, educators and policymakers. Speech and language disorders encompass a range of issues, including difficulties with articulation, fluency, voice and the ability to understand and use language effectively. These disorders can significantly affect a child’s ability to engage in the classroom. For instance, a child with a language disorder may struggle to follow verbal instructions, understand complex sentences or grasp new vocabulary. This can lead to difficulties in reading comprehension, writing, and participating in class discussions. Articulation disorders, where children have trouble pronouncing sounds correctly, can make their speech difficult to understand. This often results in children feeling self-conscious, leading to reduced participation in classroom activities and discussions. Fluency disorders, such as stuttering, can cause interruptions in the flow of speech, making it challenging for children to express their thoughts clearly and confidently. One of the most significant impacts of speech and language disorders is on literacy development. Reading and writing are foundational skills for academic success, and children with speech and language disorders often find these areas particularly challenging. Difficulty with phonological awareness – the ability to recognize and manipulate sounds in words – can hinder reading development. Children may struggle with decoding words, leading to poor reading fluency and comprehension. Writing can also be problematic. Children with language disorders may have trouble organizing their thoughts and using appropriate vocabulary and grammar. This can result in written work that is unclear and lacks detail, affecting their performance in assignments and exams. The academic struggles faced by children with speech and language disorders often extend beyond academics, affecting their social and emotional well-being. Communication is key to forming and maintaining relationships, and children who struggle to express themselves or understand others may experience social isolation. They may find it hard to make friends, join in play, or participate in group activities, leading to feelings of frustration, anxiety and low self-esteem. Early identification and intervention are critical in helping children with speech and language disorders succeed academically. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) play a vital role in assessing and treating these disorders. They work with children to improve their speech and language skills through targeted therapy, helping them to communicate more effectively. In the classroom, teachers can support these children by using clear and simple instructions, visual aids, and providing additional time for tasks. Collaborative efforts between SLPs, teachers and parents are essential to create individualized education plans (IEPs) that address the specific needs of each child. These plans may include accommodations such as speech therapy sessions, modified assignments and alternative communication methods. Schools and communities must work together to provide a supportive environment for children with speech and language disorders. Training teachers to recognize the signs of these disorders and implement effective strategies in the classroom is vital. Additionally, raising awareness among peers about the challenges their classmates face can foster a more inclusive and understanding school culture. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

Speech and language disorders – hidden barrier to academic success By Katie Pengilly For many children, the journey through school is a time of discovery, learning, and growth. However, for those with speech and language disorders, this journey can be fraught with challenges that impact their academic performance and overall school experience. Understanding the profound effects these disorders have on a child’s educational journey is crucial for parents, educators and policymakers. Speech and language disorders encompass a range of issues, including difficulties with articulation, fluency, voice and the ability to understand and use language effectively. These disorders can significantly affect a child’s ability to engage in the classroom. For instance, a child with a language disorder may struggle to follow verbal instructions, understand complex sentences or grasp new vocabulary. This can lead to difficulties in reading comprehension, writing, and participating in class discussions. Articulation disorders, where children have trouble pronouncing sounds correctly, can make their speech difficult to understand. This often results in children feeling self-conscious, leading to reduced participation in classroom activities and discussions. Fluency disorders, such as stuttering, can cause interruptions in the flow of speech, making it challenging for children to express their thoughts clearly and confidently. One of the most significant impacts of speech and language disorders is on literacy development. Reading and writing are foundational skills for academic success, and children with speech and language disorders often find these areas particularly challenging. Difficulty with phonological awareness – the ability to recognize and manipulate sounds in words – can hinder reading development. Children may struggle with decoding words, leading to poor reading fluency and comprehension. Writing can also be problematic. Children with language disorders may have trouble organizing their thoughts and using appropriate vocabulary and grammar. This can result in written work that is unclear and lacks detail, affecting their performance in assignments and exams. The academic struggles faced by children with speech and language disorders often extend beyond academics, affecting their social and emotional well-being. Communication is key to forming and maintaining relationships, and children who struggle to express themselves or understand others may experience social isolation. They may find it hard to make friends, join in play, or participate in group activities, leading to feelings of frustration, anxiety and low self-esteem. Early identification and intervention are critical in helping children with speech and language disorders succeed academically. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) play a vital role in assessing and treating these disorders. They work with children to improve their speech and language skills through targeted therapy, helping them to communicate more effectively. In the classroom, teachers can support these children by using clear and simple instructions, visual aids, and providing additional time for tasks. Collaborative efforts between SLPs, teachers and parents are essential to create individualized education plans (IEPs) that address the specific needs of each child. These plans may include accommodations such as speech therapy sessions, modified assignments and alternative communication methods. Schools and communities must work together to provide a supportive environment for children with speech and language disorders. Training teachers to recognize the signs of these disorders and implement effective strategies in the classroom is vital. Additionally, raising awareness among peers about the challenges their classmates face can foster a more inclusive and understanding school culture. Supt. Last spring, the Highlanders had one of its best seasons in coach Eric Olson’s 12 years at the school, winning the WACC regular season and advancing to the finals of the North Coast section in the post-season playoffs. They also qualified for the first time in the CIF NorCal tournament. Parker earned first-team AllLeague honors as one of its most productive batters. In 2024, Will led the team with a .375 batting average, recording 33 hits with eight doubles, He picked up 24 RBIs and scored 22 runs. PHS finished with a 19-10 record and won the Foothill regular season first-place banner with a 7-3 league record. articles.text: The 2024 Summer Olympics have officially concluded in Paris, France with the United States claiming the most gold medals and an overall medal count with 40 gold, 44 silver, and 42 bronze. China finished second with 40 gold, 27 silver, and 24 bronze, while England had the third-most medals with 14 gold, 22 silver, and 28 bronze. Last week we reported on some highlights; • Katie Ledecky became the country’s most decorated swimmer ever, • The men’s gymnastics team surprised more than a few people by winning a bronze medal, • Noah Lyles’ 100-meter win in track • Julien Alfred of tiny St. Lucia won the women’s 100 meters • A pair of sharpshooters whose video went viral. Here’s a rundown of The Posts favorite moments from this year’s Olympic Games. Stephen Curry shines in semifinals, finals Stephen Curry showed the world just how significant a basketball star he is with big performances in the Olympic semifinals and finals. He scored 36 points with nine 3-pointers in the United States’ comeback 95-91 win over Serbia, then had 24 points in the 98-87 win over France for a gold medal. It was his first Olympics appearance. Perhaps his most stunning show came with 35 seconds left in the game, hurling a shot above two pursuing defenders, then hitting his memorable ‘Night, Night’ celebration. French broadcasters were calling him “the Devil named Curry.” U.S. Women’s soccer team is back on top The United States Women’s National soccer team won the gold medal for the first time since 2012 in a heated 1-nil win over Brazil. Since failing to advance to the knockout stage for the first time in 20 years one year ago, the U.S. took an early exit from the World Cup. The U.S. dynasty was in peril without a clear path forward. But with the hiring of Emma Hayes as new head coach less than six months ago and a lineup with a half dozen new players, the U.S. won all three of its knockout stages at the Olympics with1- nil victories. They beat Japan in extra time in the quarterfinals with a spectacular goal by Trinity Rodman, then followed with another overtime win over Germany on a sweet goal by Sophia Smith. articles.text: It has nearly been a full month since the Park Fire erupted on July 24 in Butte County outside of Chico. It has burned 429,263 acres as of Tuesday, August 13, and is the fourth largest wildfire in California history. The Park Fire was classified as arson after 42-year-old Ronnie Dean Stout II pushed his burning car into a ravine. He was sentenced to 25 years to life after starting the blaze. It is the largest fire caused by arson in state history. A press release issued by Cal Fire officials stated, “As the fire was starting, an unknown male was seen pushing a car that was on fire into a gulley near Alligator Hole in upper Bidwell Park. The car went approximately 60 feet down an embankment near Chico Creek, burning completely and spreading the flames that became the Park Fire.” Wind and dry conditions helped propel the fire exponentially over the first week. The blaze picked up 124,948 acres over the first 24 hours, then exploded to 239,152 over another 24 hours. So far, Tehama County has suffered the brunt of damage with 376,322 acres, while Butte County has had 52,937 acres destroyed. Lassen National ForPhotos courtesy of CalFire The Park Fire is now the fourth largest wildfire in California history. est has lost 113,736 acres to the fire. Butte County has taken most of the property damage with 428 destroyed structures and 47 damaged. “Firefighters continued to patrol the Park Fire overnight. With no additional growth, increased containment, and improving weather conditions, the amount of remaining hot spots along the fire’s edge and potential for additional growth will continue to decrease. Firefighters on the ground continue to be assisted by the infrared capabilities of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) and aircraft to locate remaining hot spots and extinguish them. Today, firefighting resources are focused on hazard tree removal along roadways and the fire perimeter, suppression repair efforts, strengthening existing fire line, and patrol of the entire fire perimeter,” a Lassen National Forest spokesperson said, via CalFire.com. The fire had no containment from July 24-26, and is now 39 percent contained. There have even been reports of rare pyrocumulonimbus clouds, thunderclouds produced by smoke and high heat. The Park Fire has called for 5,638 personnel members, 18 helicopters, 407 fire engines, 108 bulldozers, 216 water tenders, and 128 fire crews. A total of 5,638 fire personnel have been deployed to combat the Park Fire. The Park Fire is considered arson by Ronnie Dean Stout II after pushing his burning car into a gulley.

articles.text: Exhibition ends this Sunday The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s Art of Noise exhibition ends this Sunday, August 18. The exhibit includes more than 800 artworks largely from the SFMOMA collection including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that combine design and audio. The exhibition covers more than 100 years of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org. Selected pieces from SFMOMA’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, are on view through August 18.

articles.text: New Orleans’ famous Preservation Hall Jazz Band returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium this weekend from Thursday, August 15, through Sunday, August 18. The Preservation Hall Jazz Band is a Crescent City favorite founded by tuba player Allan Jaffe in the early 1960s. They are regular performing guests at New Orleans’ JazzFest, the most-attended Jazz festival in the country and performed at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium for multiple performances. The band is now run by Jaffe’s son, tuba player Ben Jaffe, and includes singerinstrumentalist Clint Maedgen, trumpeter Brandon Lewis, pianist Kyle Roussel, drummer Walter Harris and trombonist Ronell Johnson. articles.text: Tickets now on sale for shows at the Piedmont Center for the Arts Festival Opera’s 33rd season will continue into autumn with a trio of Sunday afternoon artist recitals at the intimate Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series will launch on Sunday, September 22, at 4 p.m. with Lucky in Love presenting mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and Piedmont favorite, pianist Jeffrey LaDeur, founder of San Francisco International Piano Festival. The series will continue on Sunday, October 27, at 4 p.m. with Nothing to Fear featuring contralto Sara Couden and pianist Derek Tam. The final recital will be on Sunday, November 17 at 4 p.m. with Muses and Musings of an Impresario – a birthday celebration with special guest artists to be announced – showcasing Festival Opera General Director and baritone Zachary Gordin as well as pianist Daniel Lockert. Earlier in the company’s season, Festival Opera presented two annual Opera in the Park concerts at Orinda Community Park and Walnut Creek Civic Park, featuring beloved community park programs of grand opera and Broadway musical highlights. For the mainstage production at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin and guest stage director Céline Ricci presented a double bill of two one-act operas regarding love and betrayal: Francis Poulenc’s riveting mid-1950s monodrama La Voix humaine based on iconoclast Jean Cocteau’s play of the same name and Baroque masterpiece Dido and Aeneas by Henry Purcell, based on Virgil’s epic work, the Aeneid. Sunday, Sept. 22 at 4 p.m. Lucky in Love According to Kindra Scharich, “Lucky in Love celebrates the centennial anniversary of legendary French composer Gabriel Fauré by highlighting one of his most important song cycles: La Bonne Chanson. Inspired by his passionate love for soprano Emma Bardac and based on the exquisite poetry of Paul Verlaine, Fauré called La Bonne Chanson his “most exuberant writing.” Mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur present this work, alongside other beloved scores that explore l’amour! Sunday, Oct. 27 at 4 p.m. Nothing to Fear Contralto Sara Couden commented, “What do art, song and Halloween have in common? Well…monsters. Beasts without and within, love gone horribly wrong, generalized anxiety and existential crises, conversations with death… the world of classical music is rife with horrors, and I am excited to introduce as many of them as possible to the audience this October. I will be working with the fabulous and multi-talented pianist Derek Tam and presenting works by a list of composers including Schubert, Strauss, Wieck and Weill as well as modern composers Jordan Rutter-Covatto, Erika Oba and Chris Castro. Don’t worry, there’s nothing to fear… but fear (/love/ death/the beast within) itself.” Photos by Festival Opera Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin will be showcased in a concert in Piedmont on Sunday, November 17. Contralto Sara Couden will be featured at the PCA in Nothing to Fear on Sunday, October 27. Sunday, Nov. 17 at 4 p.m. Muses and Musings of an Impresario Baritone Zachary Gordin said, “I am honored to collaborate with this group of Bay Area treasures on this recital series and most especially to rekindle my work with the incomparable Daniel Lockert in a recital of repertoire and anecdotes that will tell a story of my journey and muses in this life of music. Songs of composers so very dear to me [will be featured]: Schumann, Mahler, Reynaldo Hahn and Jake Heggie mixed with a splash of early music and American Songbook classics.” Surprise guests are to be announced, and a birthday celebration reception including wine, bubbly and treats will follow the program. Festival Opera was founded in 1991 by Dr. Theodore Weis who twenty years earlier had helped create the Arizona Opera Company in Tucson. Past Festival Opera leadership includes the artistic direction tenures of famed soprano Olivia Stapp and Maestro Michael Morgan of the Oakland Symphony. It is currently led by Zachary Gordin. Festival Opera is committed to presenting emerging and local artists in compelling and socially relevant productions of both new and classic repertoire. Festival Opera proudly gives emerging artists a venue to hone their craft in leading roles with the guidance and collaboration of established professionals - providing a vital launching pad for their professional future. Festival alums have gone on to perform in major opera houses and symphony halls around the globe. Tickets for the Festival Opera Artist Recital Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are $40 per person for each concert, or individuals may purchase all programs for the discounted price of $95. To purchase tickets online, visit www.festivalopera.org.

articles.text: The Tony-award winning musical Evita is being performed on the San Francisco Playhouse stage now through September 7. Originally directed by Harold Prince with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, the award-winning Evita chronicles young and ambitious Eva Perón’s rise from poor illegitimate child to the most powerful woman in Latin America. The play is narrated through the lens of Marxist revolutionary Che Guevara and recounts the story of Argentina’s matriarch as she rallies the heart of a nation to bring about a new era in Argentine history. San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English said he selected Evita for the 2023-24 season because he knew it was going to be an election year in the U.S. and that democracy was certain to be on the line. “I thought, wouldn’t it be interesting to look at another time and place where a very charismatic populist leader rose up with his incredibly charismatic, popular wife to be elected to office and then, at least as the musical and some historical narratives say, began to dismantle essential elements of democracy,” English said. Sophia Alawi is cast as Eva Peron, with supporting roles by Jurä Davis, Peter Gregus, Alex Rodriguez, Albert Hodge and Chanel Tilghman. Evita is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through September 7. The venue is located at 450 Post Street, in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2023- 2024-season/evita/ or call the box office at (415) 677-9596. Sophia Alawi performs the title role in Evita at San Francisco Playhouse.

articles.text: “Three-dimensionality has always interested me,” explained Paul Bartlett, whose art exhibit is currently on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “Before embarking on my exploration of the world of ‘Xtra-Dimensions,’” I was a professor of chemistry at UC Berkeley. I taught organic chemistry and my research focused on molecules involved in natural biological processes. Gaining an understanding of these processes required the invention of new reactions and the creation of new molecules, so “design” was always a key component of my research and what I tried to teach my graduate students. The chemistry and function of the molecules we designed depended on their structures and, most importantly, their shapes in three-dimensions. Thinking in three-dimensions was thus a central feature of my academic career. While the world we all experience is three-dimensional, the photographs we take and the paintings we create are invariably displayed in a flat, two-dimensional format. It is up to us, the viewer, to recognize the depth of a forest scene, to know that a water surface is rippled and moving, maybe even to imagine patterns that are not explicitly shown. It was an attempt to break out of the constraints of a flat world that led me to explore what I call Xtra-Dimensions. My first attempts were to capture the dynamic elements of the surface of Lake Tahoe - not just to imply the fluidity and movement of the water, but to actually show it. Presenting the image as separate components in a number of layers adds a third dimension to the piece. The layers overlap so that the complete image is recreated when viewed straight on. However, the shapes of the components and their overall pattern bring additional dimensions as well as a dynamic element, with reflections and perspectives that change with your angle of view – similar to the original scene. I found that this approach is effective for many other types of Artist Paul Bartlett images: forest scenes with overlapping foliage or trees, cityscapes or abstract images with underlying geometric patterns – in short, almost any image where additional dimensions stimulate closer inspection and the discovery of something that would be missed in a two-dimensional print. Although I’m not designing new molecules, each new image and each Xtra-Dimensions pattern is nonetheless an experiment, with all the accompanying anticipation and excitement for the outcome.”

articles.text: The title Brittany Runs a Marathon tells you all you need to know about the last twenty minutes of what proves to be a surprisingly nifty movie. But it’s what comes before the marathon that makes for a wickedly good character study of one Brittany Forgler (played with panache by Jillian Bell): New Yorker, late twenties, a bit chunky (well, maybe a lot), working as an usher at an off-Broadway theater, and living in a low rent apartment in Queens. Before there is even a hint that sweats and Converse tennies are in her future, however, there is a growing sense that she is fundamentally discontent with her life and its trajectory. She feels a bit adrift. Unmoored. And then there are her habits. If she does any serious walking, for example, it’s from the couch to the refrigerator, or to the pretzel guy who has a sidewalk cart near her digs. Weekends are for partying and casual, anonymous sex. What creates a kind of critical mass regarding her sense of ennui is when she visits her primary care doctor, complaining of an inability to focus. What she’s hoping for is a quick checkup and script for Adderall. Instead, the doc suggests that her weight just might be an issue bringing with it high blood pressure and a possible fatty liver. His prescription involves more than a pill and a glass of water; instead, he suggests a healthy diet and exercise. And, for good measure, trying to convince a nonplussed Brittany, he points to a body-mass index poster on his wall and tells her she is out of her healthy range. The idea that all body types are acceptable, given what’s at stake, is never mentioned. So, back home after a brief, tearful, sit-on-the-floor crisis, followed by a mild intervention by her landlord, Catherine (Michaela Watkins), who suggests Brit join her running group. Not going to happen, she says. Yet realizing she needs to do something, Brit grudgingly breaks out the sweats plus hightops and decides she’ll try jogging/walking around the block. That’s it. Know that Brittany Runs a Marathon is a story about running; but then it isn’t. Consider running down a nicely flat sidewalk or park path meant for walking to be the equivalent of jumping out of a plane. It’s all about the journey once you make the commitment. Like all stories that contain a physical challenge or an athletic hurdle to be overcome – the mountain to be climbed – there are elements of conditioning and endurance. It’s a no pain/no gain template allowing the individual to be fully revealed. For Rocky, it was preparing for the fight. For Brit, it is, amazingly, the N.Y. Marathon finish line. And thus begins her quest to transform not only her body but her life; a struggle that changes not only her self-image but provokes reactions from old friends, which prove just as interesting. She comes to realize that her roommate, Gretchen (Alice Lee), a self-absorbed Instagram maven, was fine with Brit being the fat sidekick, but strangely unhappy with her newly minted persona. This film is fresh and engaging, never overly sentimental and constantly surprising in its twists and turns. When Brit takes an animal housesitting job (shaggy dog in an uptown brownstone, owners on vacation), she meets Jern (Utkarsh Ambudkar), a twenty-something guy who is happily adrift and apparently has the dog sitting graveyard shift. Their interactions, oil and water, add another interesting dimension to Brit’s expanding life, disclosing her sharp wit and intelligence and how she uses her quick rejoinders as a way of remaining defended. She is also fragile and fearful and even suspicious of those who reach out. Recall that I mentioned that Brittany Runs a Marathon, while about running, is about much more. Such as how she comes to resolve that nugget of deep discontent and how these newly acquired insights seep into her daily life and impact her self-esteem. Ultimately, that’s a finish line she may never totally cross; but then who does? Brittany Runs a Marathon. Directed by Paul Downs Colaizzo. Starring Jillian Bell, Michaela Watkins, Micha Stock. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Now streaming on prime. Jillian Bell and Micah Stock in Brittany Runs a Marathon

articles.text: A scene from A Dog’s Way Home As far as the kids are concerned, A Dog’s Way Home finds the PG sweet spot and stays there. They’ll take to it like, well, ducks to water. But then, of course, it’s a story about a nifty dog named Bella and her owner, Lucas (Jonah Hauer King), a med student living with his mom, Teri Lucas and his fellow med student, Olivia (Alexandra Shipp), find Bella as a pup, living with cats and kittens under an abandoned wreck of a house, and it’s Lucas who takes the wiggly, excitable, playful pooch home. She is literally a rescue dog for the house is about to be bullA year goes by, Bella grows up, and is spotted by a villainous animal control guy, Chuck (John Cassini), who makes it his mission to catch her on the street, unleashed. He claims she’s a pit bull. Worried that Bella could be impounded and even put down, Teri and Lucas send her to stay, briefly, with relatives in Farmington, New Mexico, while they search for a place to live outside of the city limits and out of Bella is, of course, homesick, misses Lucas and Terri, and at the first opportunity makes a break for it, not realizing that she is 400 miles away from home. And so begins Bella’s great two-year adventure. It proves to be a mildly harrowing journey that involves humans, a pack of stalking wolves, two men who want to adopt her, an orphaned mountain lion cub that tags along, an avalanche, learning to survive on leftovers in garbage bins and other dicey moments. Meanwhile, Bella determinedly makes her way toward home and Lucas. Kids will love all of it. Plus the filmmakers, having adapted A Dog’s Way Home from the bestselling novel by Bruce Cameron, decide to give the film a Bella voice over (by Bryce Dallas Howard) allowing her to share her impressions of all that she encounters. No worries regarding animals talking. Kids are totally on board with anthropomorphizing animals, e.g. a Disneyesque small wooden boy and an iconic mouse. Plus humans talk to dogs all the time and swear they get an answer topped off with a wagging tail. Recall that this is a PG rated film, family friendly, with a great story. Bella meets lots of kind people along the way. Be prepared: if you don’t have a Bella at home, well, kids can be persistent. Okay, just think about. A Dog’s Way Home. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. Starring Ashley Judd, Jonah Hauer King, Edward James. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. articles.text: It was a sunny, mild afternoon on August 5th when the First Mondays Reading Group met outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park for their monthly discussion. A good turnout of 18 readers came to enjoy it. The group was there to discuss Country Girl written in 2013 by Edna O’Brien. When O’Brien’s first novel, The Country Girls, was published in 1960, it so scandalized her local Irish priest that he burned it. That didn’t stop O’Brien. She went on to write books that some say are among the best writing of the 20th Century. Country Girl is the story of the events, people, emotions, and the world of an unusual and talented person. O’Brien’s memoir starts with her birth in a grand but deteriorating house in Ireland and moves through her experiences in convent school to eloping, divorce, single motherhood, wild 60’s parties in London, and her encounters with Hollywood, pop culture, and literary personalities. There is love and unrequited love, and trips to America as a celebrated writer and the guest of Jackie Onassis and Hillary Clinton. Victoria Glendinning of The Spectator wrote of O’Brien, “… She is brave, modest, bewildered.” National Public Radio’s review said, “Country Girl is Edna O’Brien’s exquisite account of her dashing, barrier-busting, up-and-down life.” Sadly, O’Brien died last month at the age of 93 while the group was reading this memoir. The group’s discussion of Country Girl clearly showed that it appealed to some but not others. The readers generally agreed on the quality of O’Brien’s writing. They appreciated her voice, courage, intelligence, style, and the book’s structure. Some liked how she closed chapters and often set up what came next. Some were deeply touched by O’Brien’s story. One reader was “gob smacked” by her life experience. This is a story of liberation for a beautiful, Irish firebrand, born in the 1930s, who escaped the control of her country’s societal and sexual norms, the dominance of the Catholic Church in her culture and a demanding husband who didn’t want her to write, but took her money when she achieved success. For these readers, O’Brien was fully alive and constantly thinking. However for other readers O’Brien’s story was depressing and tedious. Some did not know of her before they read Country Girl and found her obituary helpful in more fully understanding her and the life she led. The book seemed to assume that the reader knew who O’Brien was, but some didn’t. They did not have this frame of reference and wondered why they should be interested in her. These dissatisfied readers felt there was not enough self-reflection to fully understand who this writer really was. The story was “a slog” for them. They couldn’t get inside the person. They wanted more “meat” to understand her. O’Brien was a reluctant memoir writer, and some readers felt this may have resulted in her not providing this understanding. Other readers thought that O’Brien’s life experiences may have kept her from wanting to provide this visibility. Additionally, O’Brien’s “name dropping” of famous friends and lovers seemed like “People magazine” content for some readers. While the readers had different opinions about Country Girl they did agree that their discussion was thought-provoking and very enjoyable. This type of conversation with differing, intelligent opinions make them glad to be members of the First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride for their September book and Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for October. After hearing summaries of three fiction candidates for November, the readers selected North Woods by Daniel Mason for that discussion. Since the first Monday in September is Labor Day, the group’s next discussion will be on September 9 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group had a great turnout of 48 walkers and three K-9 best friends for their official walk back to school on August 7. This was the last Wednesday this summer that the group could walk the three Piedmont elementary school campuses before classes began. The group was pleased Robert Lang brought Tom Bjornson to walk with them for the first time, and that Lori Rubens was back after a long absence. The walkers were also happy Judy Love invited her granddaughter, Emilia Razavi, to join them in advance of her first day as a first grader at Havens School on Monday, and the walk had some special relevance for her. The walkers went to Havens School and went into the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, where some history was shared. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in September 1907. Its population grew dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and city leaders decided to build two schools. The first school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. Havens School was expanded with Depression New Deal funds in the 1930s. A new five-classroom wing was built on the eastern edge of the grounds in 1937- 38 and an auditorium was added in 1940-42. The auditorium was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, who was Havens’ first principal and taught at the school for 20 years. Students participated in painting the ceilings of all the Piedmont school auditoriums. The theme for Ellen Driscoll’s is California history. At Wildwood, it’s U.S. history; at Beach, it’s literature. Fifth and sixth graders painted the panels in a paint-bynumber fashion before they were applied to the ceilings. A new Havens School was built at the same site in 1955. The 1910 school, which faced Bonita Avenue, was torn down. The New Deal classrooms and auditorium in the back remained, but in 2010 the school was completely rebuilt, and the 1938 classrooms were demolished. The walkers exited the auditorium and stopped outside for a group photo with young Emi at her new school. They continued to Bonita and Oakland Avenues for a long walk down to Beach School on Lake Avenue. They entered the Linda Beach Playfield at Howard Avenue and made their way to the school playground. New play structures had been installed over the summer and many young people were enjoying them. “The Lake Avenue School” was built in 1913. There were four teachers and 100 students in six grades. In 1918, the school was renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in honor of Egbert William Beach, the first Piedmonter and California officer killed in France during World War I. The rapid growth of Piedmont from 1920 to 1930 created school facility needs. Beach students were taught in cramped, wooden portables. In 1933, the buildings were condemned as firetraps and an earthquake menace. They were torn down in 1934 and replaced in two Depression-era projects. The main wing was built in 1936, and an auditorium/classroom wing was added in 1940. As part of city-wide seismic facility upgrades, Beach hosted some Havens students for the 2009-10 school year while Havens was rebuilt, and Wildwood students in 2010-11. When Beach had its renovations in 2011-12, the school temporarily relocated to Emeryville with buses shuttling students there and back. In the fall of 2012, the school re-opened with two new classrooms and new playground facilities. The walkers exited the playground on Linda Avenue and went down to Grand Avenue. They crossed Grand at Ace Hardware and walked up Wildwood Avenue to Wildwood School, which opened in 1924 and expanded from 1936 to 1940 in four Depression-era projects with new classroom buildings and an auditorium. The walkers then got a look at the newly finished Witter Field track, climbed “PE Hill,” walked through the PHS campus, and returned to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Summertime may be ending for students soon, but the weather is still perfect for picking up a new summer read. The Indie Next List has fantastic summer reading recommendations, curated by independent book store owners and staff. This list for August focuses on the best new fiction titles out there, perfect for relaxing in the shade and whisking the imagination elsewhere. The Indie Next List consists of only the newest releases with reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small bookstore culture. A Sorceress Comes to Call Fantasy “In T. Kingfisher’s retelling of the Goose Girl fairytale, there’s an emphasis on found family, and finding strength in yourself that you didn’t know you had. I would like Hester and Cordelia to be my new best friends, please and thank you.” —Cora Kelly, Bear Pond Books, Montpelier, VT The Au Pair Affair “I am head over heels in love with Burgess and Tallulah! I mean, an overprotective hockey captain that falls first and falls hard, and nicknames her gorgeous? You can’t go wrong. Tessa Bailey knows how to bring the swooning full force.” —Mandy Harris, Angel Wings Bookstore, Oxford, NC The Dead Cat Tail Assassins Fantasy “When undead assassin Eveen is contracted to kill a person who appears to be her own younger self, forbidden magics and lethal shenanigans ensue. This is a delicious, funny, unexpectedly heartwarming story with just the right amount of viciousness.” —Milo Michels, University Book Store, Seattle, WA The Bright Sword: A Novel of King Arthur Fantasy “You know a book’s good when it starts with a quote from Monty Python. I utterly loved it from the first page to the last. Witty, serious, magical, and with an amazing cast of characters, this is everything an Arthurian epic should be.” —Emily Pate, Word After Word Books, Truckee, CA Slow Dance Morrow, Romance “Shiloh and Cary quickly became two of my favorite characters ever. Rowell uses dual POV and a non-linear timeline to explore a stunning relationship between two utterly flawed, brilliantly eccentric best friends.” —Ebani Filbert, The Bookworm of Omaha, Omaha, NE The Lost Boy of Santa Chionia “Set in an isolated Italian village, this is so rich in detail, so deep in characterization, that it’s like eating dessert in a fine restaurant: savoring each bite, letting it linger on the palette. Easily one of my favorite books of the year so far!” —Pete Mock, McIntyre’s Fine Books, Pittsboro, NC Pearl “A shatteringly beautiful story of a woman’s search for answers about her mother’s disappearance. Through shifting memories, the reader moves through Marianne’s trauma and changing understanding of her mother. This aches and amazes in equal measure.” —Allyson Howard, Invitation Bookshop, Gig Harbor, WA Lady Macbeth Fiction “Lady Macbeth is the gothic fantasy retelling of my dreams! Ava Reid stuns once again with their attention to historic detail as they maintain the magic of Macbeth. This book is dreamy, lush, and had me spiraling for days after reading it!” —Haley Calvin, The Novel Neighbor, Webster Groves, MO The Lost Story Books, Fantasy “Can you feel nostalgic about a book you just read? Apparently yes, if it reminds you of when you were a child who believed in magic. Like any fairy tale, there is darkness, but only enough to make the light more brilliant.” —Laura Kendall, Second Flight Books, Lafayette, IN Nicked Historical Fiction “A truly immersive, boisterous, playful, and earnest heist story from so far in the past it becomes magical. With a writing style as elusive as the plot twists, a colorful cast of thieves and priests, and a breathless romance, it’s not one to miss.” —Bridget Fenner, BookPeople, Austin, TX The Truth According to Ember Romance “Ember is tired of her deadend job, of being broke, and never getting ahead as a Chickasaw woman. So, she lies. As these lies pile up, how can Ember be real? Emotional, witty, and tender, this debut Native rom-com is a perfect workplace romance!” —Coco Zephir, Phoenix Books, Essex Junction, VT Five-Star Stranger “A completely modern look at the way we live, regarding hurt, protection, and connection. As the protagonist tries to make himself into a blank slate so he can rent himself to strangers, the faded outline of his real self keeps threatening to peek through.” —James Crossley, Leviathan Bookstore, St. Louis, MO Catalina One World, Fiction “Catalina is such a delightful book — funny and quick-witted, but also thoughtful and heart-rending. I loved Catalina’s smart, singular voice. This is a perfect read for lovers of Lily King’s Writers & Lovers, or fans of Sally Rooney’s work.” —Shannon Guinn-Collins, Bookworks, Albuquerque, NM The Ex Vows Romance “A swoony story about two best friends finding their way back to each other after breaking up five years ago. Georgia and Eli must work together for their best friend Adam’s wedding and realize they left a lot unsaid. I had butterflies the whole time!” —Claire McWhorter, River & Hill Books, Rome, GA The Horse Fiction “Al Ward is flawed – alcoholism, a never quite good enough country guitarist and song writer. When a blind horse shows up at his isolated shack on a snowy, freezing night, the best of Al comes out. Yes, Al is flawed, but you’ll root for him.” —Karen Emmerling, Beach Books, Seaside, OR I Was A Teenage Slasher Saga Press, Horror “My heart aches for the slasher? This cannot be right. Tolly, the slasher, tells his bloody, horrific story in a voice so real and raw that you can almost hear him, as though seated right beside you, and feel every detail of his inescapable pain.” —Nancy Sims-West, Raven Book Store, Lawrence, KS Burn “In the spirit of Station Eleven, there is only one thing humankind understands when it must survive: it cannot be done alone. You read this novel and wonder how such a painful book can be so damn beautiful. Gorgeous writing meets heart-pounding thriller.” —Jessilynn Norcross, McLean & Eakin Booksellers, Petoskey, MI The Unmothers Books, Horror “Anderson beautifully blends a small-town mystery with the supernatural (and a little feminist rage) to deliver this cathartic punch of a story. If you loved the what-the-hell-is-going-on energy of classic X-Files, then read this book.” —Jennifer Martin, Tattered Cover Book Store, Denver, CO Smothermoss Books, Thriller “Beautiful, surreal, and otherworldly, I fully fell into Alering’s supernatural mystery. Their use of sound grounds the reader in Sheila and Angie’s strange and difficult life on the margins of society in some of the best writing I’ve seen.” —Amanda Scroggins, Watermark Books & Café, Wichita, KS Banal Nightmare Fiction “Banal Nightmare crackles with humanity. You may hate these feckless and at times ugly characters, or recognize yourself in them. But it’ll thrill you in its fearlessness. Either way, this will leave a mark on you. It blisters.” —Matt Nixon, A Cappella Books, Atlanta, GA Mystery Lights: Stories Books, Short Stories “Mystery Lights is a collection of dark and beautiful short stories that will leave you breathless. A woven tapestry of women and girls living their lives amongst the desert and its mysteries.” —Elisa McIntosh, The Bookstore Plus Music & Art, Lake Placid, NY Charlotte Illes Is Not a Teacher Mystery “Siegel’s humor and heart shine as we follow Charlotte to her new job as a substitute teacher at her old middle school, where she helps her new colleagues solve a mystery. Fan favorites Lucy and Gabe are back to help and their banter remains delightful.” —Andi Richardson, Fountain Bookstore, Richmond, VA

articles.text: What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Over the offseason and summer, I hit 275 pounds on benchpress, and 405 pounds on the back squat. These were huge milestones for me that I am very proud of. I have also seen my conditioning progress drastically with the help of all of our coaches. Each day they push every individual to get better, and over the entire summer everyone has seen lots of improvement. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? The two biggest pieces of advice I could give a young athlete is consistency is key. Even if you only have time for a shorter workout, do it. Every workout pays off in the long run and will help you get a little bit better each day. Second is recovery. Recovery is half the fight to becoming the best athlete you can be. Whether it’s stretching every morning and after workouts, or taking ice baths whenever you can. Both of these are key in developing your body and avoiding injuries.
